metadata.name: Allergic rhinitis (hay fever / seasonal allergies)
metadata.name_ar: التهاب الأنف التحسّسي (حُمّى القش / الحساسية الموسمية)
metadata.severity: Mild to moderate but can significantly impair sleep, school/work and quality of life; linked with asthma

overview.short_description: IgE-mediated inflammation of the nasal mucosa on exposure to allergens, causing sneezing, itching, nasal congestion and clear rhinorrhoea, often with itchy watery eyes.
overview.detailed_description: Allergic rhinitis is a very common atopic condition, seasonal (pollens) or perennial (dust mite, animals, moulds). It frequently coexists with allergic conjunctivitis and asthma ('one airway' concept). Diagnosis is clinical; treatment is allergen avoidance, intranasal corticosteroids and antihistamines, with immunotherapy for selected refractory cases.
overview.pathophysiology: Sensitisation leads to allergen-specific IgE on mast cells; re-exposure triggers mast-cell degranulation (histamine, leukotrienes) causing an early-phase reaction (sneeze, itch, rhinorrhoea) and a late-phase inflammatory response (congestion).
overview.etiology: Aeroallergens: grass/tree/weed pollens (seasonal), house dust mite, animal dander, mould spores (perennial).
overview.natural_history: Often begins in childhood/adolescence; seasonal cases follow pollen calendars; may improve or persist over years; associated with asthma and sinusitis.
overview.prognosis: Good symptom control achievable; not dangerous but affects quality of life; immunotherapy can modify disease.

prevalence.value: Very common; affects roughly 10-30% of adults and more children in many populations.

incidence.value: High and rising in industrialised settings.

epidemiology.age_groups: Onset often in childhood/adolescence; any age.
epidemiology.geographic_distribution: Worldwide; seasonal pattern varies with local pollen.
epidemiology.seasonal_pattern: Seasonal forms peak with relevant pollen seasons; perennial forms year-round.

risk_factors.lifestyle: Allergen exposure (pollen, pets, dust); urban pollution.
risk_factors.smoking: Tobacco smoke worsens symptoms and airway inflammation.
risk_factors.alcohol: Can worsen nasal symptoms in some.
risk_factors.pregnancy: May worsen/change; affects safe medication choice.
risk_factors.occupation: Occupational allergen exposure (e.g., animals, flour, latex).
risk_factors.family_history: Strong - atopy (asthma, eczema, allergic rhinitis) runs in families.
risk_factors.medications: Some drugs cause non-allergic rhinitis (e.g., ACE inhibitors, overuse of decongestant sprays - rhinitis medicamentosa).
risk_factors.previous_diseases: Asthma, eczema, allergic conjunctivitis, chronic rhinosinusitis, nasal polyps.

chief_complaints.complaint: Sneezing, itchy nose, and runny nose

symptoms.importance: Itch strongly favours allergic (vs infective) cause
Late-phase; can dominate in perennial disease

symptoms.symptom: Reduced smell, postnasal drip, fatigue/poor sleep

negative_findings.finding: No itch, no ocular symptoms, purulent discharge, fever, or facial pain
negative_findings.why_important: Points away from allergy towards infection (viral URTI / sinusitis)

negative_findings.finding: Unilateral symptoms or unilateral bloody discharge
negative_findings.why_important: Not typical of allergic rhinitis - consider tumour, foreign body, or CSF leak

history_questions.question: Are the nose and eyes itchy, and is the discharge clear and watery?
history_questions.why_ask: Itch + clear rhinorrhoea strongly suggest allergy

history_questions.question: Is there a seasonal pattern or specific triggers (pollen, animals, dust)?
Any personal/family history of asthma, eczema, or allergies?
Are symptoms one-sided, bloody, or associated with facial pain/purulent discharge?
history_questions.why_ask: Red flags for alternative diagnosis (tumour, sinusitis)

physical_examination.expected_finding: Pale, boggy, swollen turbinates with clear secretions

physical_examination.examination: General atopy signs (allergic shiners, nasal crease, eczema); chest if asthma suspected
physical_examination.expected_finding: Supportive atopic features; check for wheeze

laboratory_tests.indication: When allergen confirmation is needed (uncertain diagnosis, considering immunotherapy/avoidance)

imaging.when_needed: CT sinuses if chronic rhinosinusitis/polyps or complications suspected

diagnostic_criteria.formal_criteria: Clinical: two or more nasal symptoms (sneezing, itch, rhinorrhoea, congestion) related to allergen exposure, often with ocular symptoms and an atopic history; supported by allergen testing where needed. Classified (ARIA) by duration (intermittent vs persistent) and severity (mild vs moderate-severe).

differential_diagnosis.differences: Short-lived, sore throat, no marked itch, sometimes fever, no seasonal pattern
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Is it short-lived with a sore throat, or itchy and recurrent?

differential_diagnosis.differences: Triggered by temperature/odours; no itch/ocular symptoms; decongestant overuse
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Triggered by weather/smells rather than allergens, and no itch?

differential_diagnosis.differences: Facial pain/pressure, persistent, polyps on exam
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Persistent blockage with facial pressure and reduced smell?

differential_diagnosis.disease: Unilateral nasal pathology (foreign body, tumour, CSF rhinorrhoea)
differential_diagnosis.differences: Unilateral, bloody, or clear watery unilateral discharge after trauma
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Is it only one side, or bloody?

diagnostic_questions.question: Are your nose and eyes itchy, and is there a seasonal or specific trigger?
Are the symptoms only on one side, or is there bloody discharge?

next_best_question.question: Are there specific triggers/seasonality, any wheeze, and are symptoms one-sided or bloody?
next_best_question.expected_answers: Typical allergic pattern vs asthma overlap vs red flags
next_best_question.branching_logic: Typical allergic -> treat (avoidance + intranasal steroid/antihistamine); wheeze -> assess asthma; unilateral/bloody -> ENT referral

next_best_test.why: Response supports allergic rhinitis and treats it
Confirm allergen for avoidance/immunotherapy in unclear or refractory cases

red_flags.finding: Unilateral nasal symptoms, blockage, or bloody discharge
red_flags.immediate_action: Refer ENT to exclude tumour/foreign body

red_flags.finding: Clear watery unilateral discharge after head trauma
Nasal septal perforation or destructive lesions

referral_criteria.urgent_referral: Unilateral/bloody nasal symptoms or suspected tumour; suspected CSF leak.
referral_criteria.routine_referral: Refractory symptoms despite optimal treatment; consideration of immunotherapy; nasal polyps needing ENT; diagnostic uncertainty.
referral_criteria.emergency_referral: Rarely needed (e.g., anaphylaxis with a broader allergic reaction).

initial_management.supportive_care: Explain the allergic basis; identify and reduce allergen exposure (pollen avoidance measures, dust-mite reduction, pet management).
initial_management.medications: Canonical schema 1.3 guidance: use treatment_guidance.medication_options and its history-based safety checks. Candidate classes/options (not a prescription): Intranasal corticosteroid; Second-generation antihistamine; Topical nasal decongestant. No autonomous selection or dosing is allowed. Source IDs: ARIA_2024_25.
initial_management.lifestyle_advice: Allergen avoidance (monitor pollen counts, keep windows closed at peak times, shower/change after outdoor exposure, dust-mite measures), avoid tobacco smoke.
initial_management.follow_up: Review response and technique (nasal spray); step up/down treatment; consider referral if uncontrolled.
initial_management.legacy_medications_pre_v13: Intranasal corticosteroids are first-line for moderate-severe/persistent symptoms; oral or intranasal antihistamines for mild/intermittent or as add-on; antihistamine/mast-cell-stabiliser eye drops for ocular symptoms; short-term intranasal decongestant only (avoid prolonged use); leukotriene receptor antagonist as an option (especially with asthma). Allergen immunotherapy for selected refractory cases.

patient_education.home_advice: Hay fever is an allergic reaction in the nose and eyes to things like pollen, dust or animals. Steroid nose sprays (used correctly and regularly) and antihistamines control it well; eye drops help itchy eyes. Reduce your exposure to the trigger where you can. See a doctor if symptoms are only on one side, there is bloody discharge, or you also have wheezing/breathlessness.
patient_education.home_advice_ar: حُمّى القش تفاعل تحسّسي في الأنف والعينين تجاه مواد مثل حبوب اللقاح أو الغبار أو الحيوانات. تتحكّم بها بخاخات الأنف الستيرويدية (باستخدام صحيح ومنتظم) ومضادات الهيستامين، وتفيد قطرات العين للحكة. قلّل تعرّضك للمُحفّز قدر الإمكان. راجع الطبيب إذا كانت الأعراض في جانب واحد فقط، أو ظهر إفراز دموي، أو صاحبها أزيز أو ضيق نفس.
patient_education.prevention: Allergen avoidance measures; starting nasal steroids before the pollen season if seasonal.
patient_education.warning_signs: One-sided symptoms, bloody discharge, wheeze/breathlessness, or symptoms not responding to treatment.

prevention.vaccination: Not applicable (immunotherapy can desensitise selected patients).
prevention.lifestyle: Allergen avoidance; pre-season prophylaxis with intranasal steroids.

evidence.evidence_level: High for intranasal corticosteroids and antihistamines; high for immunotherapy in selected patients.
evidence.guideline_strength: The main diagnosis/test and treatment direction was checked against the current guidance identified by ARIA_2024_25; see evidence_review for scope and limitations. This does not verify every legacy narrative sentence.

treatment_guidance.treatment_goal: Control nasal/ocular symptoms with the least burdensome effective regimen.

Candidate classes/options (not a prescription): Intranasal corticosteroid; Second-generation antihistamine; Topical nasal decongestant. No autonomous selection or dosing is allowed. Source IDs: ARIA_2024_25.

monitoring: nasal irritation/bleeding, growth in children when prolonged, and total steroid burden
